GatorGoods

A student-only marketplace for SFSU. Built from scratch by a team of seven.

  • Python
  • Flask
  • SQLAlchemy
  • Pydantic
  • MariaDB (MySQL)
  • nginx
  • Gunicorn
  • jQuery
  • HTML / CSS
  • AWS EC2 → Render
Open the live demo

Hosted on a free tier, so the first load can take a minute while it wakes up. Front-end code is in the drop-down below.

A student-only marketplace where verified SFSU students and faculty buy, sell, and trade textbooks, dorm essentials, and more. Built from scratch by a team of seven for CSC 648, Software Engineering. I was the documentation lead and a front-end developer.

  • Search and browse: keyword search with category and price filters and sorting. Guests can browse without an account.
  • Listings: create, edit, and remove listings with photos, campus pickup locations, and course tags, and mark items as sold.
  • Accounts and trust: SFSU-email sign-up, profiles and settings, bookmarks, in-site messaging, seller ratings and reviews, and moderator approval of listings and reports.
  • Front end: Jinja-templated HTML, CSS, and jQuery pages for search, dashboards, profiles, messaging, and moderation, built for desktop and mobile.
  • Back end: a Flask app served by Gunicorn behind nginx on AWS EC2, with a 14-table MariaDB (MySQL-compatible) database modeled in SQLAlchemy and validated with Pydantic. Passwords are bcrypt-hashed, photos are stored on the server under randomized filenames, and Google Analytics tracks usage. Later redeployed on Render.

Tank Wars

      
A two-player tank battle game in Java.

      
  • Java 17
  • Swing
  • Gradle
  • Object-oriented design

      
Full source below. Go poke around, nothing explodes. Probably.

    

    

      
Two players share one keyboard and fight in an arena with solid and breakable walls. Heart-shaped bullets, five hits per life, three lives each, and a win screen with play again or quit. I built it from a bare starter repository and packaged it as a runnable JAR.

      
    
        
  • Split-screen view that follows each tank, plus a mini-map, health bars, and lives in a heads-up display.
    • 
        
  • Three selectable maps and power-ups: a shield, a speed boost, and a one-shot bullet that takes a full life.
    • 
        
  • Game loop, collision handling, and breakable walls, which took the longest to debug.
    • 
        
  • Separate classes for bullets, walls, power-ups, the HUD, map loading, input, and sound, so each part could change without breaking the rest.

Custom File System

      
A file system built from raw disk blocks, with its own shell. Team of four.

      
  • C
  • Block I/O
  • Bitmap allocation
  • Directories
  • Teamwork

      
Code is in a private course repository. Available on request.

    

    

      
A working file system on a virtual disk of 19,531 blocks of 512 bytes. It formats the volume, tracks free space, stores directories, and supports a shell with ls, cd, md, pwd, touch, cat, cp, rm, plus cp2fs and cp2l to move files in and out of Linux.

      
    
        
  • A volume control block in block 0 identifies a formatted disk and records where the bitmap and root directory live.
    • 
        
  • A bitmap marks every block used or free; deleting a file frees its blocks for reuse.
    • 
        
  • The root directory is itself a file holding an array of entries (name, location, size, type, timestamps), sized to hold at least 50.
    • 
        
  • Files go through a per-file buffer that loads blocks on demand and writes back only when modified.
    • 
        
  • Before this, I wrote my own buffered file I/O functions (open, read, close) as a standalone assignment.
    • 
      

      
My part: the formatting logic in fsInit, the volume control block and directory entry structures, additions to the bitmap code, fixing the linking errors, and the directory functions fs_setcwd, fs_getcwd, fs_isFile, fs_isDir, fs_stat, and fs_delete, plus path lookup and sections of the file I/O layer.

    

  


  

    

      
Bands4U

      
A mobile-first budgeting and savings-goal app prototype that I designed and built for CSC 642, Human-Computer Interaction.

      
  • HTML5
  • CSS3
  • JavaScript
  • SVG
  • Mobile-first
  • HCI

    

    

      
Instead of treating budgeting as a chore, the app ties everyday spending to goals like a laptop, tuition, or a trip, and shows in real time how each choice moves the finish line.

      
    
        
  • 15 navigable screens: onboarding, dashboard, quick-add expense and income, goals, insights, alerts, recurring expenses, and settings.
    • 
        
  • Goal Impact Mode: sliders for cutting dining, subscriptions, and entertainment rewrite the projected finish date as you drag.
    • 
        
  • Built by hand: an SVG donut chart and progress rings, a custom number keypad, and weekly pace guidance, all in vanilla JavaScript.
    • 
        
  • Designed on HCI principles: simplicity and progressive disclosure, visual hierarchy, immediate feedback with toasts, and error prevention through smart defaults and keypad limits.

Police Dispatch Data with Threads

      
Parallel statistics over a large binary data file, in C.

      
  • C
  • pthreads
  • mutexes
  • pread
  • Statistics

      
Code is in a private course repository. Available on request.

    

    

      
Reads a fixed-length-record file of police dispatch calls, splits the records across threads, and reports how long responses take for each call type, for the whole city and for chosen neighborhoods or districts.

      
    
        
  • Parses a header file to learn field widths and offsets, then uses pread so threads read their own slices of the file without stepping on each other.
    • 
        
  • Protects the shared results with a mutex after tracking down corrupted, run-to-run-different output to a race condition.
    • 
        
  • Switched dynamic arrays from growing by one slot to doubling capacity, which removed long freezes on the 500K-record file.
    • 
        
  • Computes min, max, median, quartiles, IQR, outlier bounds, mean, and standard deviation per call type.
    • 
      

      

        
Run time on 500K records. More threads did not mean faster: waiting on the lock cost more than the extra workers saved.

        
1 thread
3.07s

        
2 threads
5.13s

        
4 threads
4.80s

        
8 threads
4.69s

      

    

  


  

    

      
XOR Encryption Device Driver

      
A Linux kernel module that encrypts text.

      
  • C
  • Linux kernel
  • ioctl
  • Device drivers

      
Code is in a private course repository. Available on request.

    

    

      
A character device driver that registers with the kernel, accepts an encryption key through ioctl, XORs any text written to it, and returns the result when read. Because XOR is symmetric, running the same key again decrypts.

      
    
        
  • Implements the open, read, write, and release file operations.
    • 
        
  • Moves data across the user/kernel boundary with copy_from_user and copy_to_user instead of trusting user pointers.
    • 
        
  • Keeps the key (ioctl) separate from the message (write).
    • 
        
  • Fixed two bugs: encrypted newlines that broke formatting, and leftover bytes from earlier messages, solved by skipping newlines and clearing the buffer before each write.
    • 
      

    

  


  

    

      
Simple Shell with Pipes

      
A Unix-style command interpreter written in C.

      
  • C
  • fork / execvp
  • pipe / dup2
  • Linux

      
Code is in a private course repository. Available on request.

    

    

      
A shell that reads a line, splits it into arguments, launches the command in a child process, waits for it, and reports the child’s PID and exit code. It also chains commands with |, so output from one program becomes input to the next.

      
    
        
  • Reads input with fgets into a fixed 91-byte buffer, so long lines can’t overflow memory.
    • 
        
  • Tokenizes commands with strtok into the NULL-terminated array that execvp expects.
    • 
        
  • Builds every pipe before forking, wires each child with dup2, and closes unused file descriptors so processes see end-of-file correctly.
    • 
        
  • Decodes real exit codes with WEXITSTATUS instead of printing the raw status from waitpid.
    • 
        
  • Accepts a custom prompt as a command-line argument.
    •
